Package manager.d: A tool that downloads, installs, updates and removes software packages and the other packages they depend on. Examples: Homebrew, npm, pip and uv.

Dependency.d: A package your project needs in order to run or be built. Dependencies often have dependencies of their own (transitive dependencies).

Lock file.d: A file such as package-lock.json or uv.lock that records the exact version of every installed package, so everyone and every CI run gets the same set.

Semantic versioning.d: A version-number convention MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: major for breaking changes, minor for new features, patch for fixes. Often shortened to semver.

Node.js.d: A program that runs JavaScript outside the browser, on your computer or a server. Many developer tools, including Playwright, run on it.

npm.d: The package manager that comes with Node.js. It installs JavaScript packages into a project's node_modules folder and records them in package.json.

npx.d: A command that comes with npm and runs a package's command-line tool, downloading the package first if it is not installed.

Homebrew.d: A free package manager for macOS and Linux that installs command-line tools and apps with commands such as brew install.

Virtual environment.d: A self-contained folder (usually .venv) holding a Python interpreter link and its own installed packages, so each project's packages stay separate.

pip.d: Python's standard package installer. Run it as python -m pip inside a virtual environment to install packages from PyPI.

uv.d: A fast Python package and project manager from Astral that can install Python, create virtual environments, add dependencies and write a uv.lock lock file.

Python.d: A popular, readable programming language widely used for automation, data work, testing and AI applications.

Variable.d: A name that points to a value in a program, such as passed = 47.

Dictionary.d: In Python, a collection of key-value pairs written with braces, such as {"id": "QA-1"}. The Python equivalent of a JSON object.

Function.d: A named, reusable block of code that takes inputs (parameters) and usually returns a result.

Exception.d: An error raised while a program runs, such as KeyError or FileNotFoundError. It stops the program unless code catches it with try/except.

Traceback.d: Python's report of an uncaught exception: the chain of calls that led to the error, ending with the error type and message on the last line.

Timeout.d: The longest a program will wait for something, such as a server's reply, before giving up with an error.

Exponential backoff.d: A retry strategy where the wait doubles after each failed attempt (for example 0.5s, 1s, 2s), usually with a little randomness (jitter) added.

Pagination.d: Splitting a long list from an API into pages that the client fetches one at a time, using a page number, cursor or next link.

Async.d: Asynchronous code: a style (async/await in Python) where a program starts many slow operations, such as network calls, and waits for them together instead of one by one.
